title: ‘They’re Fucking a Lot of People’: 7-OH Users Brace for DEA Ban
gist: The DEA plans to place the kratom-derived opioid compound 7-OH and related synthetics MGM-15/MGM-16 into Schedule I starting August 5, 2026, and dependent users, clinicians, and quality-testing data all point to a messy, high-risk transition for an unregulated market that had scaled via gas-station retail and social-media ads.

insights.claim: The DEA plans to place 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and the related compounds MGM-15 and MGM-16 into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act — the same category as heroin — via a temporary order taking effect August 5, 2026 at the earliest, lasting two years with an option to extend one more year while the agency pursues permanent scheduling.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Sets a hard regulatory deadline (Aug 5, 2026) that eliminates a supplement category with an active national consumer base almost overnight, a template worth watching for other unregulated psychoactive-supplement categories.
insights.locator: But all that is in jeopardy now, as the Drug Enforcement Administration plans to place 7-OH

insights.claim: A dozen U.S. states had already banned 7-OH before the DEA's federal action, showing state-level prohibition was already running ahead of federal scheduling.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: State-by-state bans preceding federal action is a recurring pattern for emerging unregulated substances/products; state activity can be a leading indicator of eventual federal crackdown.
insights.locator: Already, a dozen states have banned 7-OH.

insights.claim: The DEA's stated rationale for the ban is that 7-OH is an opioid agonist with high abuse potential being marketed to consumers as a botanical dietary supplement, a category the FDA does not vet for safety or efficacy before it reaches the market.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Highlights the regulatory gap (unvetted dietary-supplement status) that let a potent opioid-like compound scale to mass retail before enforcement caught up — a structural loophole other novel psychoactive products could still exploit.
insights.quote: Given its pharmacological profile as an opioid agonist and high abuse potential, the marketing of 7-hydroxymitragynine products to consumers as botanical supplements constitute a significant public health risk
insights.locator: reads the DEA's notice of intent about the proposed ban

insights.claim: The federal ban emerged from a split between the mainstream kratom industry, which argues 7-OH is too potent to count as kratom, and 7-OH producers/proponents who say it can't be separated from kratom — and the Trump administration sided with the kratom lobby by targeting 7-OH specifically.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Regulatory outcomes in nascent, unregulated substance markets can be shaped by which incumbent lobby wins political favor rather than purely by safety data — relevant to handicapping future scheduling fights.
insights.locator: The DEA's action comes amid a wider rift between the mainstream kratom industry

insights.claim: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, both officials WIRED reports have strong ties to the kratom industry, publicly championed the 7-OH crackdown — Kennedy calling the 7-OH industry 'sinister' and claiming products are 'marketed for children' via brightly colored gummies.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Potential conflict of interest between officials driving a specific enforcement action and the industry segment (kratom) that benefits from it — a governance risk factor for how the ban's scope was drawn.
insights.locator: Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy called the 7-OH industry

insights.claim: Because natural kratom only contains trace amounts of 7-OH, the plant itself will not meet the threshold to be captured by the DEA's ban, structurally insulating the larger existing kratom market from this specific enforcement action even though 7-OH is derived from the same plant.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A narrowly drawn ban that exempts the larger incumbent category (kratom) while eliminating a smaller, faster-growing derivative (7-OH) is a pattern investors in supplement/nutraceutical-adjacent categories should watch for in other scheduling actions.
insights.locator: Because kratom—a Southeast Asian plant that has analgesic properties

insights.claim: One long-term 7-OH user spends around $500 a month buying the compound in bulk online, while another user was spending $175 every four to five days (roughly $1,000+/month) at the height of his use before quitting, illustrating steep tolerance-driven cost escalation.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Shows real per-user spend levels in the unregulated 7-OH market — useful for sizing the addressable consumer base and the economic disruption a ban creates for dependent users.
insights.locator: Cam has turned to buying it in bulk online, spending around $500 for an order

insights.claim: 7-OH has scaled through mainstream retail (gas stations and smoke shops nationwide) and targeted social-media advertising, including at least one user who was served a free-sample Instagram ad — a fast, low-friction customer-acquisition model typical of unregulated consumer products before enforcement catches up.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Retail ubiquity plus paid social ads let a Schedule-I-bound opioid-like compound reach mass consumer distribution rapidly; a repeatable growth pattern for emerging unregulated categories worth flagging early.
insights.locator: he says he was served an Instagram ad for a free sample of 7-hydroxymitragynine

insights.claim: Ahead of the August 5 ban, some users who can afford it are stockpiling 7-OH rather than planning to quit, indicating a likely demand and price spike for remaining legal supply in the weeks before enforcement begins.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A pre-ban stockpiling rush is a predictable, trackable short-term demand spike in the legal 7-OH market and its online sellers.
insights.locator: In advance of the ban, some people who can afford it and don't want to quit are stockpiling

insights.claim: A pharmacy-student user's 7-OH brand received an 'F' grade on third-party lab testing for being stronger than advertised and for containing undisclosed MGM-15 — a potent synthetic opioid derivative not listed on the product label.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of potency mislabeling and undisclosed synthetic-opioid content in unregulated 7-OH products — a core safety justification regulators can point to, and a due-diligence red flag for anyone evaluating supplement-adjacent categories.
insights.locator: When he checked out the brand he'd been using on a third-party testing site

insights.claim: Multiple 7-OH users interviewed by WIRED say they want the product better regulated — with accurate testing, clear addiction-risk labeling, and removal from gas-station shelves — rather than banned outright, suggesting latent demand for a regulated middle path instead of prohibition.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A regulated-but-legal pathway (dosing standards, mandatory testing, age-gated sales) is the alternative outcome users themselves are advocating for, relevant if the temporary Schedule I order is later softened or challenged.
insights.quote: How can a developed nation like the United States have products on the shelf that do not contain what the labeling states it contains, whether it be melatonin or whether it be 7-OH?

insights.claim: Petros Levounis, chair of psychiatry at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, says he now sees a handful of ER patients a month seeking help with kratom or 7-OH withdrawal, and that clinicians still lack an established, 7-OH-specific detox protocol, instead adapting standard opioid-withdrawal treatment.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Rising ER-level withdrawal cases without a standardized treatment protocol signals a real, growing public-health burden that a ban alone won't resolve, and points to buprenorphine-based detox demand.
insights.quote: it's still quite a novel substance. We haven't fully wrapped our heads around how to treat it best.
insights.locator: Doctors use a similar detox protocol to opioid withdrawal

insights.claim: Levounis says he isn't opposed to a federal ban in principle but doubts it will have much impact, implying the underlying self-medication demand for chronic pain and anxiety will persist and likely shift elsewhere rather than disappear.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A clinician's skepticism that prohibition solves the underlying demand is a useful counter-signal to the DEA's stated public-health rationale for the ban.
insights.locator: While Levounis doesn't think a federal ban is a bad idea

insights.claim: Several interviewees, including long-term user Cam, fear that once the legal 7-OH supply disappears under the ban, dependent users will relapse into street opioids like heroin or fentanyl, potentially driving a spike in overdose deaths — an unintended consequence of the scheduling action.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A ban-induced relapse-to-street-opioids pathway is a specific, trackable public-health risk metric (overdose rates) to watch in the months after the August 5 effective date.
insights.locator: he fears that will be the case for many 7-OH users once the ban kicks in

insights.claim: Cam, a chronic-pain patient who says 7-OH replaced his prescription oxycodone and helped him stay off alcohol and street opioids, describes the DEA's looming ban as devastating and blames the agency directly for the harm it will cause dependent users like him.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Puts a human face on the policy trade-off: for some chronic-pain patients, 7-OH functioned as an accessible substitute for prescription opioids, so removing it abruptly carries direct relapse/pain-management risk for that user segment.
insights.quote: They're fucking a lot of people. It's caused me so much anxiety.
